idiom_name: std::sync::RwLock<T> + Arc; read()/write() return Deref guards
implementation_notes: std::sync::RwLock<T> owns the data it protects: read()/write() hand out RAII guards that Deref (and DerefMut) into T, so the 'which lock protects which fields' question disappears. Readers hold shared guards, writers get exclusive access; a writer panic poisons the lock (later lock() calls return PoisonError) and the priority policy is the operating system's, so writer starvation is possible and the documentation warns that read-then-write in one thread can deadlock. Choose it for ordinary thread-based services; use parking_lot when poisoning and fairness must be predictable, and tokio's RwLock when the readers and writers are async tasks.
pitfalls: Never hold a std::sync::RwLock guard across .await: the guard is not Send-friendly in async contexts and a blocking lock inside a task stalls the runtime.
The documented deadlock: thread A takes read(), thread B waits for write(), A takes a second read() - the second read may block behind B and the thread deadlocks.
Poisoning must be handled deliberately; .unwrap() on a poisoned lock turns one writer panic into a cascade of reader panics.
Write starvation is OS-dependent and unspecified; a steady reader stream can postpone a writer indefinitely on some platforms.

variants.name: parking_lot::RwLock (task-fair, no poisoning)
variants.implementation_notes: A drop-in replacement with a task-fair policy: readers block when writers wait (so recursive read locking can deadlock by design), write locks can be downgraded atomically, the lock is one word, there is no poisoning, and uncontended acquisition is an inline fast path - typically faster and more predictable than std. It is a crate dependency, and its fairness contract becomes part of your API contract.
pitfalls: Recursive read locking can deadlock by design: readers yield to waiting writers.
No poisoning means a panicked writer leaves the data in an unknown-but-accessible state; validate invariants yourself.
Its fairness policy is a crate guarantee, not the OS's - do not casually mix expectations with std::sync::RwLock in one codebase.

variants.name: tokio::sync::RwLock (async tasks)
variants.implementation_notes: For async tasks: read().await/write().await yield instead of blocking a thread, and the lock is deliberately fair and write-preferring (a FIFO queue prevents writer starvation), which differs from std's OS-dependent policy. blocking_read()/blocking_write() exist for synchronous contexts and owned guards (read_owned/write_owned) let a lock travel with a spawned task; never hold a std RwLock across .await and never call the blocking_* methods from async code.
pitfalls: Using std::sync::RwLock in async code (or tokio's blocking_read from a task) blocks runtime threads and can deadlock the executor.
The fair queue means a burst of writers delays all readers; that is intentional but changes throughput under mixed load.
Borrowed read()/write() guards cannot outlive the borrow - use read_owned()/write_owned() with Arc for spawned tasks.
